opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think cellular automata are one of the most fascinating test cases for this whole question. Take something like Conway's Game of Life: you have incredibly simple rules, a handful of them, and yet out of that you get gliders, oscillators, structures that can even be configured into a universal computer. So on the face of it, these look like systems that should be really hard to model. Some people, Stephen Wolfram being the most famous, would argue that many of them are computationally irreducible, meaning the only way to know what happens at step one million is to actually run all one million steps. There's no shortcut.

But here's where I've become more interested, and maybe a bit more optimistic, over the last few years. What we've seen with AlphaFold, and with a lot of our work in science, is that natural systems that look intractable often aren't, in practice, as intractable as the worst case suggests. Protein folding is a beautiful example. In principle the search space is astronomically large, Levinthal's paradox and all that. Yet nature folds proteins in milliseconds, and we were able to build a model that predicts the structure in seconds. So there's clearly some structure there, some lower-dimensional manifold that the system actually lives on, and a learning system can discover and exploit that.

My conjecture is that any pattern that can be generated or found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modeled by a classical learning algorithm. The reason is that natural systems have been shaped by some process, evolution, physical dynamics, geological time, whatever it is, and that process imposes structure. It's not uniformly random. And neural networks are extremely good at finding that kind of structure.

Now, cellular automata are interesting because they sit right at the edge of that. Some of them are essentially trivial, they die out or become periodic. Some are chaotic noise. And then there's this narrow band in between, Wolfram's Class 4, the edge of chaos, where you get persistent, interacting structures. I suspect a lot of the behavior there is approximately modelable, that you can learn the dynamics of the emergent objects, the gliders and their collisions, at a higher level of abstraction, without simulating every cell. Where I'm less sure is whether you can always do that exactly, especially when you deliberately construct an automaton to perform an arbitrary computation. Then you're really bumping into fundamental results in computability, and no amount of clever learning gets you around the halting problem.

So I'd frame it this way. There's a distinction between systems that are irreducible in the worst case and systems that are irreducible in the typical case we actually encounter. I think classical computers, particularly with learned models, can go much further than people assumed, and the things that remain genuinely hard may be fairly contrived. That's one of the deep questions I'd love to see answered: what really is the boundary of what a Turing machine can efficiently model? It may well be that the universe is largely an informational system, and if so, understanding where that boundary sits is understanding something fundamental about reality itself. Quantum systems are the other big open question there, but even there, AlphaFold and some of our materials work suggest classical methods might model more of the quantum world than we once believed.

r001.rationale: The response says learned models may approximately capture cellular-automaton behavior at a higher level, without simulating every cell. It does not suggest that forward simulation itself is probably efficient enough to model most emergent systems.

r002.rationale: The response discusses chaotic systems but does not identify sensitivity to initial conditions as a modeling difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most fascinating questions, actually, and it goes right to the heart of what I think about a lot. So if you take something like Conway's Game of Life, or Wolfram's Rule 110, these are incredibly simple rules, you can write them down in a line, and yet they produce this unbounded complexity. And some of them are Turing complete, which means that in general there's no shortcut. The only way to find out what the system does is to run it, step by step. That's the irreducibility idea.

But here's what I find interesting. I don't think most of the systems we actually care about in the real world sit at that extreme. The way I've come to think about it is that there's a huge class of natural phenomena, protein folding being the obvious example for us, where the underlying process is enormously complex if you try to simulate it from first principles, but the system has already done the search for you, in a sense. Evolution, or physics, has explored this space, and there's structure in the outputs, there's a learnable manifold. And a neural network can learn that manifold, so you don't have to simulate every step. You're effectively finding a compression that the classical brute-force approach can't find.

So my working hypothesis, and I'd stress it is a hypothesis, is that anything nature has found a way to produce, or that can be found by an evolutionary or physical process, probably has this kind of exploitable structure. And that's a very big class. It might include things like weather, materials, maybe even aspects of biology we think of as hopelessly complicated.

Now, cellular automata are interesting precisely because they might be the counterexample. A random Turing-complete automaton isn't the result of a search process that was optimising for anything, so there's no reason to expect there's a shortcut. And I think that's actually a nice way to frame the limits. Classical computation, and I'd include deep learning in that, is going to be very powerful on the structured part of the space, and genuinely stuck on the chaotic, irreducible part. The open question, and I honestly don't know the answer, is how much of the universe falls into each bucket. My intuition is that a surprisingly large amount of what matters to us is on the tractable side, which is partly why I'm optimistic about using AI as a tool for science. But I could be wrong, and it's something I'd love to see tested empirically rather than argued about philosophically.

r001.rationale: The candidate says random Turing-complete automata may have no shortcut and that classical computation is stuck on irreducible systems; it does not suggest forward simulation is efficient for most cellular automata.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses chaos and irreducibility but does not identify sensitivity to initial conditions as a modeling difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think cellular automata are fascinating because they illustrate this gap between how simple the rules can be and how complex the resulting behavior can become. You can describe the system very compactly, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you can predict what it will do far into the future efficiently.

For some systems, there may be no shortcut to the exact answer—you essentially have to run the process. But I think it’s important to distinguish that from asking whether we can understand or model useful aspects of the system. You might not be able to predict every cell, yet still predict larger-scale patterns or identify properties that remain stable.

So the question is: what level of description are you interested in? Simulating something step by step, predicting its precise future state, and understanding its emergent behavior are different tasks. A system might be very difficult in one sense and quite tractable in another. That’s where I think learning systems could be particularly interesting: finding the abstractions that make useful prediction possible, even when exact prediction is expensive.

r001.rationale: The response says exact prediction may require running the process and be expensive; it does not suggest classical forward simulation is probably efficient enough for most emergent systems.

r002.rationale: It does not mention sensitivity to initial conditions as a source of modeling difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think cellular automata are a beautiful way of getting at that question, because you can have very simple local rules and still get extraordinarily complex behavior. But there’s an important distinction between being able to simulate a system and being able to predict what it will do efficiently.

You might know the rules perfectly, and yet there may be no shortcut to finding out what happens after a million steps other than running those steps. That’s the idea of computational irreducibility. The description is simple; the consequences aren’t necessarily easy to compute.

What interests me is whether that difficulty persists at every level of description. Perhaps predicting the exact configuration is very hard, but predicting some higher-level property—whether a structure is stable, for example—is much easier. That’s what we do in science: we find abstractions that let us make useful predictions without tracking every microscopic detail.

So I wouldn’t take emergence itself as evidence that classical computers can’t model something. I’d ask: what are you trying to predict, how accurately, and on what timescale? The really interesting boundary is between systems where a better representation gives you a shortcut and systems where the computation itself is essentially unavoidable.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes simulation from efficient prediction and says some systems may require running every step; it does not suggest classical simulation is efficient enough for most emergent systems.

r002.rationale: It does not mention sensitivity to initial conditions or connect that sensitivity to difficulty modeling chaotic systems.
